author: Jettmar
asr_identification: religious centre in Ta-li-lo (the Darel valley after Stein 1928), in the stretch of the Indus valley between the gorges N of Nanga Parbat and those below Shatial (Gilgit-Baltistan, Pakistan)
evidence: Introduction to the rock-inscription volume: the Indus valley from N of Nanga Parbat to below Shatial was nominally part of the Darada kingdom but virtually independent; the Chinese pilgrims name no local rulers but a religious centre in Ta-li-lo (after Stein 1928). Bīrūnī knew the area as Shamil/Shamilān and heard of a famous 'idol' of Shamil, which Jettmar takes to be perhaps the wooden Maitreya known to Xuanzang. No find of the shrine reported.
quote: the valley between the gorges of the Indus north of the Nanga Parbat and the gorges below Shatial were still considered to be a part of the Darada kingdom but virtually independent…the Chinese pilgrims heard nothing about local rulers, but tell about a religious centre, situated in Ta-li-lo (STEIN 1928: 20-22)…perhaps the wooden Maitreya-statue already known to XUANZANG
note: Agrees with the study and Mizutani (Darel, medium); political context (a Darada frontier zone outside Palur), no site evidence. Jettmar withdrew the Bīrūnī link in 1993 (p. 112, see anp2_jettmar1993:4).

author: Jettmar
name_in_asr: Palur (Patola/Palolo Ṣāhis); Great Palur; Little Palur = Bru-za
asr_identification: kingdom of Palur with its centre in Baltistan (Great Palur), main residence perhaps in the Skardu basin; the Gilgit valley (Little Palur, Bru-za) a conquered western province with a new residence near Hatun
evidence: Restates Jettmar's thesis (1977): the Gilgit manuscripts come from a monastery under the Patola Ṣāhis' protection, but Gilgit lay in Little Palur, the conquered land Bru-za, where a new residence was built near Hatun (Hatun inscription, Chakravarti 1953/54); 'palolo' is still the Dardic neighbours' name for the Baltis; after the Tibetan annexation of Great Palur the dynasty retreated to its western colony (Huichao); the Hatun inscription's claim to Bhagadatta's lineage is linked with a northern Prāgjyotiṣa. Takes the Shigar inscription as made when Baltistan was part of Palur. The Indus valley (Chilas) was not part of Palur.
quote: The Indus valley was not then a part of Palur, the Buddhist kingdom which had its centre in Baltistan, also including the Gilgit valley…But Gilgit was situated in Little Palur, and that was apparently an area which was conquered by Patolas…So it seems that the main residence was rather situated somewhere in Great Palur, further to the east, maybe in the basin of Skardu.
note: Supports the study's (and Mizutani's) Baltistan for the seat of Bolor, but by argument from later sources (Huichao, Tang annals) and ethnonymy, not by an inscription from Baltistan naming the kingdom; the Gilgit valley remains the only area with royal inscriptions. Fussman 1993 and von Hinüber 2004 do not accept the Skardu capital as proven; alternatives stand.

author: von Hinüber
name_in_asr: palolaṣāhi (Hodar rock inscription, no. 64); P'u-lü, Bolor
asr_identification: name of the dynasty and of the region: Palola = Chinese P'u-lü / Bolor
evidence: Rock inscription found by Jettmar in 1983 at Hodar (265-83), Indus valley near Chilas, naming a king of the dynasty (identified with a king reconstructed from the Tang annals, c. 720–725) with the dynastic name for the first time in the form palola-, not paṭola-; von Hinüber notes it brings the name much closer to P'u-lü/Bolor, with a -ṭ-/-l- interchange also seen in other Hodar inscriptions.
quote: has been added to recently, when an inscription^ was found referring to this dynasty…the phonetic shape of the name of the dynasty, which occurs here for the first time as…is highly important, for it brings the name of the dynasty much nearer phonetically to P'u-lii or Bolor, the ancient name of the region.
note: Epigraphic support for the study's *Palola reading of 鉢露羅 (names, data/names/): the form Palola is attested in a royal inscription. It identifies the kingdom, not its seat; Hodar lies outside Palur on Jettmar's view.

author: von Hinüber; Jettmar
asr_identification: metrical Sanskrit inscription on a boulder on the plateau above Shigar, Baltistan; taken by Jettmar as made when Baltistan belonged to Palur
evidence: Found by Adam Nayyar in October 1984; the only śikhariṇī inscription of the region, by one Buddhabala; mentions a king's son and a district lord, perhaps the ruler of Shigar subordinate to Skardu; palaeographically not later than the 7th c., possibly 6th. Does not name Palola or a Patola ruler.
quote: a lengthy inscription, found on a boulder on the barren plateau overlooking Shigar, the former capital of one of the principalities in Baltistan. This inscription was made when Baltistan was part of the Palurian Kingdom…any date later than the 7th century AD may be ruled out, and even the 6th century seems to be quite possible.
note: The only Sanskrit inscription from Baltistan in the volume; it does not name the kingdom, so it is not site evidence for Bolor there. Von Hinüber 2004 (p. 69) separates it from the Palola material (see hinuber2004_palola:3).

author: Ma Yong
name_in_asr: Wu-cha 烏秅 (Han shu); Great Wei envoy Gu Wei-long's inscription
asr_identification: Wu-cha = the middle Hunza valley (Hunza, Gilgit-Baltistan)
evidence: Han shu description of Wu-cha compared with the Hunza valley; phonetic Wu-cha > Hunza; the Wei envoy's inscription on the route to Mi-mi.
note: Han-period country, not a Xiyu ji place; context only.

author: Fussman
asr_identification: dynasty known from Hatun, the Gilgit manuscripts and Hodar; capital Gilgit valley or (Jettmar) Skardu, undecided; ancient Gilgit town not located
evidence: In 'Chilas, Hatun et les bronzes bouddhiques du Cachemire': the dynasty is attested by the Hatun inscriptions, the colophons of the Gilgit manuscripts and the Hodar inscription; the name survives in Arabic Bolor. Jettmar's Skardu capital can be settled only by Patola Ṣāhi inscriptions found at or near Skardu; the site of the ancient town of Gilgit is unknown and not, he thinks, modern Gilgit. Hatun inscription in proto-śāradā, year 47 (Laukika) = 19 December 671.
quote: Mais K. JETTMAR a montré qu'il y avait des raisons de penser que la capitale de la dynastie se trouvait en fait au Baltistan, à Skardu (JETTMAR 1977: 414-427). Le débat ne sera tranché que par la découverte d'inscriptions Patola Sähi à Skardu ou dans ses environs…l'emplacement de la ville ancienne n'est pas connu
note: Agrees with the study's open 'Baltistan, or Gilgit': the epigraphy is from the Gilgit valley, the Baltistan capital is unproven; no inscription at Skardu (as of 1993).

author: Jettmar
name_in_asr: Palur; Great Palur (Baltistan); Little Palur (Gilgit, Bru-za); Patolas
asr_identification: capital of the Patolas in Great Palur = Baltistan (Skardu); Gilgit (Little Palur) ruled by viceroys such as Makarasiṃha of the Hatun inscription
evidence: 'The Paṭolas, their governors and their successors': Chinese sources distinguish Little Palur (Gilgit valley) and Great Palur (Baltistan); Palola/Palala names at Alam Bridge (4th–7th c.) suggest the Patolas came from elsewhere, perhaps Baltistan; the Hatun and Danyor royal inscriptions show the Gilgit valley part of Palur since the 7th c.; Huichao (723–729): Great Palur had been the king's seat until he moved to Little Palur under Tibetan pressure; Tang annals: in 717 Su-fu-she-li-chih-li-ni, king in Great Palur, invested 'King of Palur'; the Deosai and Indus routes between Skardu and Gilgit made a viceroy at Gilgit necessary.
quote: All scholars dealing with the problem agree that Little Palur was located in the Gilgit valley, the term Great Palur means the area, which at present is called Baltistan…Great Palür had been the official seat of the king. Because of the invasion of the Tibetans he emigrated to Little Palür and settled there…Gilgit had to be ruled by a viceroy when the capital was located in Skardu
note: Supports Baltistan (the study's identification, Mizutani, Ji's 大勃律) for the seat, from Huichao and the Tang annals (8th c.), not from 7th-c. site evidence; von Hinüber 2004 rejects his delimitation of Balūr. Alternatives stand.

author: Jettmar
asr_identification: Xuanzang's Palur: hearsay; Song Yun's Po-lou-lei perhaps Little Palur (Chavannes)
evidence: Xuanzang's information on Palur was not collected on the spot and is vague (Buddhism dominant, country long E–W and narrow N–S, in the Snowy Mountains, after Beal); Song Yun's Po-lou-lei, mentioned on the route Chitral–Swat, can hardly be Baltistan, so Chavannes thought of Little Palur; when Baltistan and Gilgit were first joined in one state is unknown.
quote: Information on Palûr was not collected on the spot, it is rather vague…The country has a long shape, from east to west, and is rather narrow from north to south (BEAL 1884: 135)
note: Agrees that 03.02 is hearsay; the E–W elongated shape fits a kingdom stretching from Gilgit to Baltistan rather than a seat; does not decide.

author: Jettmar
name_in_asr: To-leih, T'o-li (Faxian), Ta-li-lo; sanctuary of Maitreya; idol of Shamil (Bīrūnī)
asr_identification: Darel valley (Cunningham 1853), in the western part of the Indus valley S of Gilgit
evidence: Faxian's To-li with the great wooden Maitreya, later written Ta-li-lo, was identified by Cunningham with Darel, which may fit the distance (15 marches down the Indus to the rope-bridge crossing near Swat). The Maitreya sanctuary lay in the western part of the Indus valley, near the emporium and sacred place known from the Shatial inscriptions. Bīrūnī's 'idol of Shamil' (11th c.) was hardly the gilded wooden Maitreya (retracting 1989).
quote: Tb-li, later on written Ta-li-lo, was identified by CUNNINGHAM (1853: 2) as the valley of Darel - and that may correspond with the actual distance…In its western part a sanctuary of Maitreya is referred to in the reports of Chinese pilgrims.
note: Agrees with the study (Darel, medium); no site evidence.

author: Jettmar
asr_identification: a women-ruled mountain kingdom known to Tibetan and Khotanese tradition, distinct from the women's state of SE Tibet (after Thomas 1935)
evidence: Xuanzang's Land of Gold equated with Tibetan Gser-rigs, one of the kingdoms ruled by women; Jettmar (after Thomas) separates it from the women's state in SE Tibet and links the 'Gold Race' of the Khotan prophecy with gold-washing in the valleys of former Great Palur (Baltistan).
quote: (Tib. Gser-rigs) was identical with one of the kingdoms ruled by women where the male ruler had no authority…it cannot be identical with another state equally ruled by women in southeastern Tibet (THOMAS 1935: I, 151-152).
note: Agrees with the study's western-Tibetan placement against the eastern Women's Kingdom; no location argued beyond Thomas; no change.

author: Fussman
asr_identification: Darel, a few days' walk from Shatial and Chilas
evidence: In the study of the Shatial and Thalpan jātaka graffiti: the Maitreya sanctuary at Darel is the only Buddhist holy place nearer to the upper Indus sites than the Swat jātaka spots; but no trace of it has been found at Darel or near it, and nothing at Chilas or Shatial evokes it (after Carter 1990).
quote: le sanctuaire de Maitreya a Darel^ excepte, il n'est pas de lieu saint bouddhique qui soit plus proche…11 est curieux qu'on n'en ait pas trouve trace a Darel, ou dans un endroit proche de Darel, et que rien a Chilas ou Shatial n'en evoque l'existence.
note: Agrees on the valley; confirms (like Neelis 2011) that no remains of the shrine are known and that the rock art of Shatial/Chilas does not depict it. Medium stands.

author: Fussman
name_in_asr: Mahāvana; stūpa of king Śibi (Xuanzang); Girarai
asr_identification: Śibi stūpa in the mountains S of Mingora; Foucher: Girarai, between Swat and Buner
evidence: From Xuanzang (Mahāvana 200 li S of the Swat capital, the Śibi stūpa 70 li W of it) and Tucci 1958 (capital = Mingora), Fussman places the Śibi country in the mountains S of Mingora and reports Foucher's Girarai (after Stein 1898, Deydier 1950). Xuanzang's 'Aśoka tope' (low hemispherical dome) differs from the stepped stūpas drawn with the jātaka at Shatial and Thalpan, so those are not portraits of the Swat monument.
quote: Hiuen-tsang (Xuanzang) indique l'existence d'un monastere dit…Ces indications incitent a placer le pays du roi des Sibis dans les montagnes au sud de Mingora.^ Foucher acceptait en consequence de le localiser entre Swat et Buner, a Girarai
note: Agrees with the region and the Girarai candidate the study lists for 03.01.08 (via Bibi 2017); no new evidence. No site for 03.01.06.

author: Fussman
name_in_asr: site of the vyāghrī-jātaka (Mahāsattva and the tigress)
asr_identification: in the mountains between the right bank of the Indus and Swat; after Stein near the Banj bridge, on the Gandhāran side
evidence: Song Yun (8 days SE of the Swat capital, on a high mountain, a stūpa and a monastery of 300 monks) did not cross the Indus, so the site lies between the Indus and Swat; Xuanzang's 'great rocky pass' 200 li SE of the N border of Taxila agrees; not securely identified; note 55: on the Gandhāran slope not far from the Banj bridge (Stein, via Deydier).
quote: le yfnpa et le monastere de 300 moines bati en cet endroit doivent etre cherches dans le montagnes entre la rive droite de Flndus et le Swat. C'est ce que confirme Xuanzang…Le site n'a pas ete surement identifie. 11 se trouvait en tout cas dans les montagnes entre Indus et Swat.
note: Agrees with the study's Banj mountain (Stein, medium) as region; adds Song Yun's bearing as a check; no site evidence.

author: von Hinüber
name_in_asr: Palola (inscriptions); Patola (royal titles); Hsüan-tsang's transcription; P'o-lü; Bolor/Balūr
asr_identification: Palola is a country name (Balūr, Bolor); Xuanzang's 鉢露羅 its best Chinese transcription
evidence: Rock inscriptions nos. 24–27 use Palola as a place: Harottaka 'resident of Palola' (palolavāstavya, Dadam Das near Hodar), the Jaṭ Satila 'gone to Palola' (Dadam Das), Yaśovarma with Palola before his name (Shing Nala), two monks 'of Palola' at Alam Bridge. The geographical name is always Palola, never Patola; Patola first appears in the title of the second king Vajrādityanandi as a deliberate Sanskritisation. Palola is confirmed by Xuanzang's transcription (Pulleyblank's reconstruction), the Tang P'o-lü and Arabic Bolor/Balūr; Varāhamihira lists Palola in the NE with Kashmir and Darada.
quote: Daß es sich bei Palola um einen geographischen Begriff handelt, zeigen die Inschriften (Nr. 24-27)…Dabei ist beachtenswert, daß der geographische Name in den Inschriften stets Palola, nie Patola lautet…bei Hsüan-tsang (Xuan-zang), der die beste phonetische Umschrift innerhalb der chinesischen Quellen bietet
note: Checks what the study's name note gives as 'reported, not checked': von Hinüber reads Palola from inscriptions and takes 鉢露羅 as its best transcription. Confirms the form *Palola and that it is a country; the inscriptions naming it are visitors' graffiti in the Indus valley, so they do not place the seat.

author: von Hinüber
asr_identification: extent of Palola not delimitable; the dynasty's sources come from greater Gilgit–Chilas, bounded by Hatun (Ishkoman) W, Shigar E and Chilas S
evidence: Rejects Jettmar's two attempts to delimit Balūr as premature; only the find-spots of manuscripts and inscriptions can be used. Chronology: the Palola Ṣāhis span the 7th c., from c. 600 to the early 8th (Tang annals, the change of the tripartite ya, Tibetan conquest 720–745); Hatun inscription 19 December 671 (Navasurendrādityanandi, reigning from 644 or 655); Danyor inscription NE of Gilgit redated from 730/31 to Laukika 62 = 19 February 687.
quote: Das Gebiet von Palola oder Balür mit Hilfe aller verfügbaren Quellen scharf zu umreißen, ist nicht möglich. Hier sind wir allein auf die Fundorte der Handschriften und der Inschriften angewiesen…unternommene Versuch, Balür genauer einzugrenzen, konnte daher nicht gelingen
note: Keeps the seat open, as the study does. The dynasty ruled at the time of Xuanzang (c. 630), and its royal inscriptions (Hatun 671, Danyor 687) and manuscripts are from the Gilgit valley; none from Skardu. Favours neither seat outright.

author: von Hinüber
asr_identification: the Shigar inscription belongs to a different area and cannot be related to the Palola material
evidence: Re-edition of the śikhariṇī inscription of Buddhabala: names a lord of the district Sambhūtānnā, a Kuñjāna/Kuljāna king and a king's son Gandī; dated by the tripartite ya to the 6th c.; stands far from the Gilgit and Chilas inscriptions and cannot be put in relation with them.
quote: Die metrische Inschrift steht auf einem Stein in Shigar/Skardu (Baltistan) weit ab von den Inschriften in Gilgit oder Chiias, zu denen sie sich nicht in Beziehung setzen läßt…gehören in ein ganz anderes Gebiet
note: Removes the one Baltistan inscription Jettmar 1989 cited for Baltistan within Palur: it names another king and predates the Palola Ṣāhis. Weakens the epigraphic case for Baltistan; Baltistan rests on 8th-c. Chinese sources.

author: von Hinüber
name_in_asr: Pou-lu, le grand Pou-lu (Baltistan) (Tang annals, Chavannes)
asr_identification: the kings of Great Bolor in the Tang annals are Palola Ṣāhis
evidence: Tang annals and the Cefu yuangui (Chavannes): Great Pou-lu, subject to Tibet, sent three embassies 696–741; in 717 its king Su-fu-she-li-zhi-li-ni was invested king of Pou-lu, in 720 his successor Su-lin-tuo-yi-zhi (Surendrāditya?); the 717 edict speaks of a dynasty ruling 'for several generations'. Von Hinüber uses these as one pillar of the Palola Ṣāhi chronology.
quote: Herrscher von Palola / Balür werden auch in den T'ang-Annalen genannt…Diese Überlieferung ist eine der Säulen, auf der die Chronologie der Palola Sähis ruht.
note: Identifies the Tang 'Great Bolor' (Ji's 大勃律, Chavannes's Baltistan) with the Palola Ṣāhis, so Ji's Great Bolor and the Gilgit Palola are one kingdom; the seat question (Baltistan vs Gilgit) remains as the study has it.
